name: Standard
blurb: General world trivia: music, movies, history, science, places and more.

clues.q: This band from Liverpool featured John, Paul, George and Ringo.
Michael Jackson’s 1982 album featuring “Billie Jean” and “Beat It” shares its name with its title track.
Which composer wrote the “Moonlight Sonata”?
This K-pop group’s 2020 single “Dynamite” was its first song recorded entirely in English.
This Puerto Rican artist released the 2022 album “Un Verano Sin Ti.”
This 1997 James Cameron film about a doomed ocean liner starred Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet.
In this 2013 Disney animated film, Queen Elsa sings “Let It Go.”
This 2019 Bong Joon-ho film became the first non-English-language film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture.
This Hayao Miyazaki film, about a girl named Chihiro trapped in a world of spirits, won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature at the 2003 ceremony.
This 2021 South Korean Netflix drama follows cash-strapped contestants competing in children’s games for a huge cash prize.
This ancient civilization along the Nile built the great pyramids at Giza.
Julius Caesar was assassinated on the 15th day of the third month in 44 BCE, a date known by this Roman name.
clues.a: What are the Ides of March?

clues.q: This Greek city-state, home of the Parthenon, is often called the birthplace of democracy.
This Chinese philosopher, who lived around 551–479 BCE, had his sayings collected in the Analects.
This king of Macedon conquered the Persian Empire and founded a famous Egyptian port city named after himself.
In 1969, this American astronaut became the first person to walk on the Moon.
This barrier dividing a German city fell in November 1989.
Nelson Mandela became president of this country in 1994.
This international organization was founded in 1945 and has its headquarters in New York City.
In 1997, the United Kingdom transferred sovereignty over this territory to China.
This is the largest ocean on Earth.
Canberra is the capital city of this country.
Mount Everest is part of this Asian mountain range.
Africa’s most populous country, it has Abuja as its capital.
This narrow strait runs through Istanbul, dividing the city between Europe and Asia.
H₂O is the chemical formula for this substance.
Because of its rusty color, this planet is nicknamed the Red Planet.
Often called the “powerhouse of the cell,” these organelles produce most of a cell’s energy.
This metallic element has the chemical symbol Fe.
This English scientist set out his three laws of motion in the 1687 book “Principia.”
Known as the “Queen of Pop,” this singer released “Like a Virgin” in 1984.
This singer-songwriter named her 2014 album “1989” after her birth year.
This Jamaican reggae legend fronted the Wailers and sang “No Woman, No Cry.”
This K-pop girl group’s members are Jisoo, Jennie, Rosé and Lisa.
This Italian Baroque composer wrote “The Four Seasons,” a set of four violin concertos.
This boy wizard with a lightning-bolt scar is the title character of a film series that began in 2001.
In Disney’s 1994 film “The Lion King,” this young lion is the son of Mufasa.
Who directed the 1993 dinosaur blockbuster “Jurassic Park”?
This 2018 romantic comedy set in Singapore was based on a Kevin Kwan novel.
In this 1954 Akira Kurosawa film, a village hires a group of warriors to defend it from bandits.
Gladiators fought in this huge amphitheater in Rome, completed around 80 CE.
Stretching across northern China, this enormous line of fortifications was built and rebuilt over many centuries.
clues.a: What is the Great Wall of China?

clues.q: This last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt was allied with the Roman general Mark Antony.
This Greek mathematician’s name is attached to the theorem a² + b² = c².
This Babylonian king is known for a law code carved on a stone stele around 1750 BCE.
This civil rights leader delivered the “I Have a Dream” speech in Washington, D.C., in 1963.
clues.a: Who is Martin Luther King Jr.?

clues.q: In 1991, this country dissolved into 15 independent states.
First released by Apple in 2007, this device combined a phone, a music player and an internet communicator.
This country gained independence from Britain in 1947, with Jawaharlal Nehru as its first prime minister.
Launched by the Soviet Union in 1957, this was the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth.
The Margherita, topped with tomato, mozzarella and basil, is a classic version of this Italian dish.
This Japanese dish pairs vinegared rice with ingredients such as raw fish.
Guacamole is made mainly from this green-fleshed fruit.
This Korean side dish of fermented vegetables is most often made with napa cabbage.
This spice, harvested by hand from the stigmas of a crocus flower, is among the most expensive by weight.
This ocean giant is the largest animal living on Earth today.
This black-and-white bear native to China eats mostly bamboo.
This spotted big cat is the fastest land animal.
This Australian marsupial sleeps much of the day and feeds almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves.
This is the only group of mammals capable of true powered flight.

questions.q: How many sides does an octagon have?
Boiling point of water at sea level, in °C?
Players per side on the field in soccer?
Smallest planet in our solar system?
Mineral rated 10, the top of the Mohs hardness scale?

clues.q: This Austrian composer of “The Magic Flute” died in 1791 at age 35.
clues.hint: A child prodigy born in Salzburg.

clues.q: Fronted by Freddie Mercury, this British band released “Bohemian Rhapsody” in 1975.
clues.hint: The band’s name is a royal title.

clues.q: This Colombian singer of “Hips Don’t Lie” co-headlined the 2020 Super Bowl halftime show with Jennifer Lopez.
clues.hint: Her name begins with “Sh.”

clues.q: This Compton rapper won the 2018 Pulitzer Prize for Music for his album “DAMN.”
clues.hint: His other albums include “To Pimp a Butterfly.”

clues.q: Which Russian composer wrote the ballet “Swan Lake”?
clues.hint: He also wrote “The Nutcracker.”

clues.q: This 1977 film written and directed by George Lucas introduced Luke Skywalker and Darth Vader.
clues.hint: “A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away…”

clues.q: This nickname for the Hindi-language film industry based in Mumbai blends the city’s former name with a famous American one.
clues.hint: Mumbai was once called Bombay.

clues.q: Ang Lee’s 2000 martial-arts epic starring Chow Yun-fat and Michelle Yeoh won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film.
clues.a: What is Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon?
clues.hint: Its title names two animals in hiding.

clues.q: Based on George R. R. Martin’s novels, this HBO fantasy series ran from 2011 to 2019.
clues.hint: “Winter is coming.”

clues.q: This 1941 Orson Welles film centers on a newspaper tycoon’s mysterious dying word, “Rosebud.”
clues.hint: Title is the tycoon’s name with a civic word before it.

clues.q: Julius Caesar’s adopted heir Octavian became Rome’s first emperor and in 27 BCE took this honorific name meaning “venerable.”
clues.hint: A summer month is named after him.

clues.q: This Mauryan emperor of India embraced Buddhism after the bloody Kalinga War.
clues.hint: His lion capital is India’s national emblem.

clues.q: This volcano’s eruption in 79 CE buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum.
clues.hint: It overlooks the Bay of Naples.

clues.q: This ancient Mesopotamian writing system used wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay tablets.
clues.hint: Its name comes from the Latin for “wedge.”

clues.q: During the Second Punic War, this Carthaginian general famously crossed the Alps with war elephants.
clues.hint: He crushed a Roman army at Cannae in 216 BCE.

clues.q: Following the Watergate scandal, this U.S. president resigned in 1974.
clues.hint: He was the 37th president.

clues.q: This tense 13-day standoff in October 1962 between the U.S. and the Soviet Union centered on nuclear weapons in the Caribbean.
clues.a: What is the Cuban Missile Crisis?
clues.hint: Named for the island where the weapons were placed.

clues.q: This currency was launched for electronic payments in 1999, with banknotes and coins following in 2002.
clues.hint: Its symbol is €.

clues.q: In 1989, while working at CERN, this British computer scientist proposed the World Wide Web.
clues.hint: He was knighted; his initials are T. B.-L.

clues.q: This 1955–56 protest in an Alabama city began after Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat.
clues.a: What is the Montgomery bus boycott?
clues.hint: Riders stayed off public transit in the state capital.

clues.q: FIFA organizes the World Cup for this sport.
clues.hint: Played with feet and a round ball.

clues.q: In 2009, this Jamaican sprinter set the 100-meter world record of 9.58 seconds.
clues.hint: His surname sounds like lightning.

clues.q: The martial art of taekwondo originated in this country.
clues.hint: Same country as hapkido and ssireum.

clues.q: This city hosted the 2008 Summer Olympics, opening with a ceremony on 8/8/08.
clues.hint: Home of the “Bird’s Nest” stadium.

clues.q: This is the highest rank in professional sumo wrestling.
clues.hint: Holders wear a thick white rope in ring-entering ceremonies.

clues.q: “Konnichiwa” is a common greeting in this language.
clues.hint: Also says “arigatou” for thanks.

clues.q: This Korean alphabet was created in the 15th century under King Sejong the Great.
clues.hint: South Korea celebrates it with a holiday every October 9.

clues.q: Pinyin is the official system for writing this language in the Latin alphabet.
clues.hint: The most widely spoken language in China.

clues.q: The national language Filipino is based mainly on this language.
clues.hint: Spoken natively in and around Manila.

clues.q: L. L. Zamenhof published this constructed international language in 1887.
clues.hint: Its name means “one who hopes.”

clues.q: Nicknamed the “King of Rock and Roll,” this singer recorded “Heartbreak Hotel” and lived at Graceland.
clues.hint: Born in Tupelo, Mississippi.

clues.q: This Swedish pop group won the 1974 Eurovision Song Contest with “Waterloo.”
clues.hint: Its name is a palindrome of initials.

clues.q: The gentle, jazz-influenced style called bossa nova originated in which country?
clues.hint: Think “The Girl from Ipanema.”

clues.q: In 2012, this PSY hit became the first YouTube video to reach one billion views.
clues.hint: Named after an upscale Seoul district.

clues.q: This German Baroque composer wrote the six “Brandenburg Concertos.”
clues.hint: His surname is a German word for “brook.”

clues.q: In this 1939 film, Dorothy and her dog Toto follow the yellow brick road.
clues.a: What is The Wizard of Oz?
clues.hint: “There’s no place like home.”

clues.q: This 2017 Pixar film follows a boy named Miguel during Mexico’s Día de Muertos.
clues.hint: Named after Miguel’s great-grandmother.

clues.q: This long-running British sci-fi series about a time-traveling alien first aired in 1963.
clues.hint: Travels in a blue police box called the TARDIS.

clues.q: Starring Michelle Yeoh as a laundromat owner, this multiverse film won Best Picture at the 2023 Academy Awards.
clues.a: What is Everything Everywhere All at Once?
clues.hint: The title covers all things, all places, all times.

clues.q: This 1958 Alfred Hitchcock thriller starring James Stewart topped Sight & Sound’s 2012 critics’ poll of the greatest films.
clues.hint: Its title is a word for a spinning, dizzy sensation.

clues.q: This ancient Greek poet is traditionally credited with the “Iliad” and the “Odyssey.”
clues.hint: Shares a name with a famous cartoon dad.

clues.q: The Rosetta Stone helped scholars decipher these ancient Egyptian picture symbols.
clues.hint: Name comes from Greek for “sacred carvings.”

clues.q: This founder of the Achaemenid Persian Empire captured Babylon in 539 BCE.
clues.hint: Shares an epithet with Alexander.

clues.q: This ruler unified China in 221 BCE and was buried with the Terracotta Army.
clues.hint: His dynasty’s name may be the root of “China.”

clues.q: This Bronze Age civilization of South Asia included the planned cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro.
clues.a: What is the Indus Valley Civilization (Harappan Civilization)?
clues.hint: Named for a great river in modern Pakistan.

clues.q: Many feared computer systems would fail when dates rolled over to the year 2000 because of this bug.
clues.hint: Three characters; “K” stands for thousand.

clues.q: This Princess of Wales died in a car accident in Paris in 1997.
clues.hint: Mother of Princes William and Harry.

clues.q: In 1953, this Sherpa mountaineer and Edmund Hillary became the first to reach the summit of Mount Everest.
clues.hint: First name begins with T.

clues.q: In 1964, this city hosted the first Summer Olympics held in Asia.
clues.hint: It hosted the Summer Games again decades later.

clues.q: In 1965, this city-state became an independent nation after separating from Malaysia.
clues.hint: Its symbol is the Merlion.

clues.q: This wrought-iron lattice tower was built for the 1889 World’s Fair in Paris.
clues.hint: Named after the engineer whose company built it.

clues.q: Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built this white marble mausoleum in Agra in memory of his beloved wife.
clues.hint: It stands on the south bank of the Yamuna River.

clues.q: This 15th-century Inca citadel sits high in the Andes of Peru.
clues.hint: Name means “old peak” in Quechua.

clues.q: This Art Deco statue with outstretched arms overlooks Rio de Janeiro from Corcovado mountain.
clues.hint: Completed in 1931, it was voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007.

clues.q: This 12th-century temple complex appears on the national flag of Cambodia.
clues.hint: Near the city of Siem Reap.

clues.q: This is the star closest to Earth.
clues.hint: You see it every day.

clues.q: This gas giant is the largest planet in our solar system.
clues.hint: Famous for its Great Red Spot.

clues.q: This planet is famous for its bright ring system and its large moon Titan.
clues.hint: Sixth planet from the Sun.

clues.q: Launched in 1990, this orbiting observatory is named after an American astronomer whose first name was Edwin.
clues.a: What is the Hubble Space Telescope?
clues.hint: Its namesake proved that galaxies exist beyond our Milky Way.

clues.q: In 1961, this Soviet cosmonaut became the first human to travel into space.
clues.hint: Flew aboard Vostok 1.

questions.q: Which gas do plants absorb from the air for photosynthesis?
How many interlocking rings appear on the Olympic flag?
Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States?
What is the smallest prime number?
In which country is the city of Marrakesh?
By weight, what is the largest organ of the human body?
How many keys does a standard modern piano have?
Which ocean lies between Africa and Australia?
Which gas makes up most of Earth’s atmosphere?
Which Shakespeare play contains the line “To be, or not to be”?

rounds.name: Final Round
rounds.q: This Portuguese-born explorer died in the Philippines in 1521, but the survivors of his Spanish expedition completed the first circumnavigation of the globe in 1522.
rounds.hint: A strait near the southern tip of South America bears his name.

rounds.name: Final Round
rounds.q: In 1877, German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen popularized the name for this ancient network of trade routes linking China with the Mediterranean world, named after a prized fabric.
rounds.hint: The fabric comes from the cocoons of a certain caterpillar.
